analysis.one_liner: Gives the FTC and state attorneys general new power to go after COVID-19 scams and price gouging.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let the FTC and state attorneys general sue over COVID-19-related fraud and unfair pricing, never got a committee hearing or a vote before the term ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During the pandemic, scammers sold fake cures, bogus test kits, and overpriced masks, and ran schemes tied to stimulus checks and unemployment benefits. This bill would have given the Federal Trade Commission a specific legal tool to treat such practices as violations of consumer protection law, and let state attorneys general sue in federal or state court for injunctions, penalties, and refunds for residents. It was introduced in July 2020, sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who bought COVID-19-related products or were targeted by pandemic-related fraud: the bill would have empowered the FTC and state attorneys general to stop the practices and win refunds and penalties.

how_it_helps.text: Treats unfair or deceptive acts tied to the COVID-19 emergency as violations of FTC consumer protection rules, covering goods advertised as pandemic-related, goods with sharply increased demand, and schemes tied to testing, treatment, stimulus checks, and unemployment insurance [S2][S3].

Lets state attorneys general sue in federal or state court to stop violations, obtain civil penalties, and win damages or restitution for state residents, while explicitly preserving stronger state consumer protection laws [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Sellers who engaged in unfair or deceptive practices around pandemic-related goods and services, including fraudulent marketers and sellers charging inflated prices during shortages; legitimate businesses would have faced the cost of compliance and defending FTC or state actions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sellers of COVID-related goods and services

drawbacks.text: The standard covers goods with sharply increased demand, not just outright fraud, so it could have reached lawful price increases by sellers responding to shortages, forcing them to defend FTC or state actions [S3].

Both the FTC and state attorneys general could pursue the same conduct, and the bill layers a new federal cause of action on top of existing state consumer protection laws, adding compliance and legal costs for businesses selling pandemic-related products [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit was real but time-limited to the emergency, and the FTC already had general authority against fraud; the bill's main added value was speed, the explicit demand-surge trigger, and state enforcement muscle. The main cost, the risk of sweeping in legitimate price increases during shortages, is a genuine design weakness but one courts would have had to sort out. On balance, a modest, targeted consumer protection measure.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Ben Ray Luján introduced the bill on July 23, 2020, with 12 Democratic cosponsors, all from the House [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce; that was the only action the bill ever received [S5][S1].
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate action followed, and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sellers of COVID-19-related goods and services faced no new FTC or state enforcement authority: no one is better off among consumers, but no new liability was imposed on pandemic-era sellers, and the status quo of general FTC fraud authority remained in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pandemic-era sellers faced no new liability

for.name: Ben Ray Luján
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to give the FTC and state attorneys general authority over COVID-19-related unfair and deceptive practices [S1][S3].

for.role: Original cosponsors (Butterfield, Kennedy, Loebsack, McNerney, Cardenas, Grijalva, Case, Pascrell, Norton, Welch, O'Halleran, Veasey)

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the committee controlled by Democrats did not advance the bill [S3][S4][S5].

industries.industry: Sellers of pandemic-related consumer goods (masks, sanitizers, test kits)
industries.note: The bill would have exposed them to FTC and state lawsuits for unfair or deceptive conduct, including pricing tied to surging demand. Consumers paid inflated prices during shortages, so the industry's interest in unregulated pandemic pricing ran against buyers.
The bill's core target: schemes around fake cures, bogus testing, stimulus checks, and unemployment benefits would have carried penalties and restitution for victims.
The bill granted them a new federal cause of action with penalties and restitution powers for state residents, expanding their enforcement toolkit.
The FTC gained an emergency-specific standard for COVID-19-era practices on top of its existing consumer protection authority, and an intervention right in state suits.
